Updated assessment incorporating SLOOS: The FOMC stance remains clearly accommodative and growth-supportive (ELB policy rate, ongoing Treasury and agency MBS purchases). The May 2021 FSR still tempers the outlook with risks around stretched valuations, CRE fragilities (especially CMBS), and nonbank funding vulnerabilities, though bank capital remains strong.

The July 2021 SLOOS points to a meaningful improvement in credit intermediation that reinforces policy transmission and offsets some FSR caution:
- Banks reported stronger C&I loan demand across large, middle‑market, and small firms, alongside higher inquiries; many eased C&I loan terms.
- Reasons cited for easing included an improved economic outlook, competition, and better risk/liquidity/capital positions.
- Consumer credit standards eased (credit card, auto, and other consumer loans).
- Residential real estate: demand for Qualified Mortgages strengthened; GSE‑eligible standards largely unchanged; few subprime originations.
- CRE: multifamily lending standards eased.
- U.S. branches/agencies of foreign banks saw stronger C&I demand, tied to financing inventory, accounts receivable, capex, and M&A (though some terms remained unchanged).

Netting these, the SLOOS indicates both stronger loan demand and easier supply, consistent with accommodative financial conditions and improving credit flow to households and businesses. This tilts the overall read more positive than a policy‑only or FSR‑weighted view, while still acknowledging macro‑financial vulnerabilities.
